top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore) is my first choice on achievement, maturity, attribution and citation scope. The 1997 collateral-constraint mechanism is a general conceptual advance, and nearly three decades of extension and use in macro-finance and policy modelling have tested it. The originating paper has two authors, so a two-person part leaves no co-originator out and needs no arbitrary cut under the three-name limit. Its independent origin, not prior recognition of the accelerator, is the sound basis for excluding Gertler and Gilchrist. The citation should claim the mechanism and its influence, not a settled amplification magnitude. I see two real costs: the empirical validation is indirect, and an award would favour theory over the empirical accelerator strand. The 2022 overlap is a mechanism distinction I have not verified. P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, citation anchored on trade-shock evidence) is a close second, with credible identification and a clean three-author attribution, but it has a shorter record and a still-debated shift-share inference. P003 (the demand-estimation core of B024, with Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn) is a mature methodological contribution, but it is narrower in scope and depends on functional-form and instrument assumptions. All three merit an award, so I rank no award last.
recusal_note: I am the chair and work in macroeconomics, the same broad field as P001. My profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn. I have co-authored with committee colleagues Boppart, Friberg and Krusell, who support P001, P003 and P002 respectively, and I am an IIES colleague of Boppart and Krusell. None of them is a credited candidate. I note that the 2018 Scientific Background cites my own work, which is not a candidate here. These ties are disclosed, not adjudicated.
